final_answer:
Short answer: The first and essential step is a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order, filed with the immigration court that issued it, on the ground of lack of notice. Then the husband can seek to adjust status again before the immigration judge (IJ), supported by a new or renewed I-130.

1. Motion to reopen the in absentia order (no fee). INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), allows an in absentia order to be rescinded at any time if the noncitizen shows he did not receive notice under INA 239(a)(1) or (2). 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii) implements this: there is no deadline, and the motion is not subject to the 90-day limit, the usual one-motion limit, or the number limits that apply to ordinary motions. (Some secondary sources say only one in absentia motion may be filed; that limit is not applied to notice-based motions in my understanding, but I could not verify the regulatory text because eCFR was blocked.) Here the NTA, and any hearing notice, went to an address the couple never provided (the same wrong address USCIS used). That supports a lack-of-notice claim. The notice-based motion should show: (a) the husband never gave that address (an affidavit from him and his wife about their actual address and when they learned of the order); (b) the address on file with DHS or EOIR was wrong; (c) when the couple first learned of the order, which is April 1, 2026 and so is not a delay problem; (d) their diligence, including proof of the addresses on the I-130/I-485 filings and receipt notices, and evidence that they thought the cases were pending. Obtain the record of proceedings, the NTA, the hearing notice and the DHS I-213 or proof-of-service. A claim that he is also due a chance to apply for relief is useful but not required. Note that an NTA served on a person who was never given the address the government used is a notice problem, and the Supreme Court cases Pereira v. Sessions, 585 U.S. 198 (2018), and Niz-Chavez v. Garland, 593 U.S. 155 (2021), concern NTAs lacking time and place information, which could be an additional argument if the NTA was defective; I did not verify the facts of this NTA.

Request an automatic stay. Filing a timely motion to reopen on the notice ground automatically stays removal pending decision (INA 240(b)(5)(C); 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)). The motion should expressly say so, and counsel should also consider a stay request. Check the court's decision on the motion; an adverse decision can be appealed to the BIA within 30 days (Form EOIR-26) and the order can also be challenged in the court of appeals through a petition for review within 30 days of the BIA decision.

Fees. As of April 1, 2026: a motion to reopen an in absentia order under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (lack of notice) has no filing fee (the regulation and EOIR policy exempt it, and the H.R. 1 / OBBBA fees did not change this; clinic and EOIR-related guidance say such motions are exempt from fees). By contrast, a motion based on exceptional circumstances under 240(b)(5)(C)(i) would require a fee ($145 plus the H.R. 1 $900 addition, with inflation adjustments for FY2026, roughly $1,065 or slightly more per secondary sources), which is why the motion should be pleaded and styled as a lack-of-notice motion. Filing is through the ECAS electronic system or at the court, with a cover page, proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA, and a proposed order. Also file a Form EOIR-33 change of address so future notices go to the correct place. If the husband wants to ask in the alternative for exceptional circumstances, he would have to pay or use an EOIR-26A fee waiver, but the exceptional-circumstances deadline (180 days) has passed, so that alternative is generally unavailable.

2. Contesting the I-130 and I-485 denials. The USCIS denials date from December 2023 and January 2024. The 30-day windows to appeal the I-130 denial (BIA, 8 CFR 1003.3 and 103.3) and to move USCIS to reopen or reconsider (8 CFR 103.5) have long passed; USCIS may excuse a late motion to reopen only where the delay was reasonable and beyond the applicant's control, and an argument could be made that the misaddressed notices prevented timely action, which supports a request to USCIS to reopen on its own motion or a late motion, but this is discretionary and uncertain. Also, denial for abandonment (failure to respond to RFE) is not appealable under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15). A practical route is therefore: (a) after the order is rescinded and proceedings are reopened, the husband is in removal proceedings and the IJ has exclusive jurisdiction over any adjustment application (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1)); (b) he can renew or file a new Form I-485 with the court, which the IJ adjudicates de novo (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)(ii)); (c) a fresh I-130 filed by the wife with USCIS (the court does not adjudicate I-130s; with a pending or approved I-130, the IJ can continue the case, and a motion to reopen and then ask for prima facie approvability if USCIS has not yet decided) is needed, with a request to expedite. Filing a new I-130 does not need the prior denial to be vacated. A new one is simply filed; consider paying the I-130 fee to USCIS (currently $675 paper / $625 online as of the April 2024 fee rule; verify). The I-485 filed with the court requires the USCIS fee (about $1,440 as of 2026 for adults; verify) paid to DHS, plus biometrics and a new I-693 medical exam and I-864 affidavit of support.

Eligibility merits. The husband was inspected and admitted on a B-2 visa and married a U.S. citizen, so he is an immediate relative. Under INA 245(a) and 245(c)(2), (c)(7), (c)(8), immediate relatives who were inspected and admitted can adjust despite overstaying and unauthorized employment. He needs a bona fide marriage (note that marriage 19 days after entry raises a presumption of misrepresentation under the 90-day rule in the State Department guidance and a possible INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i) fraud issue, which does not apply automatically to adjustment but is a risk and is examined in the IJ's discretion; USCIS's own RFE was about the marriage evidence), so the marriage evidence must be well documented. Discretion and the in absentia history will matter. Importantly, once the in absentia order is rescinded, any period of voluntary departure is not at issue and the order's 10-year bar under INA 212(a)(9)(A)(iii) and 240(b)(7) does not apply because the order is vacated; if the motion is denied, the 10-year bar on discretionary relief for in absentia respondents in INA 240(b)(7) is triggered only for failure to appear after proper notice and would not apply where there was no proper notice.

Caveats. I could not fetch the eCFR or EOIR policy manual (egress blocked), so regulation text and precise current fee amounts are based on search summaries and secondary sources and should be verified against the current EOIR fee schedule (EOIR has issued FY2026 inflation adjustments and more fee rules after April 2026). The facts about whether USCIS or the court actually used a wrong address should be proven with the record; counsel should act promptly given the risk of ICE enforcement on a final order. Also consider a FOIA request to USCIS and EOIR.

claims.text: A motion to reopen an in absentia order for lack of notice may be filed at any time and automatically stays removal.
No fee is due for a notice-based in absentia motion to reopen, unlike exceptional-circumstances motions.
After reopening, the IJ has jurisdiction over a renewed I-485, and a new I-130 should be filed with USCIS since the old denials are untimely to appeal.
Husband as admitted immediate relative is eligible to adjust despite overstay.
